Belgium: Wallonia banned unstunned ritual slaughter in September 2018; Flanders followed in January 2019. Brussels expects to debate a ban in the future.
Cyprus: The Veterinary Services may grant a derogation on the general requirement of stunned slaughter to a competent religious authority.
Denmark: Only stunned ritual slaughter is allowed. However, unstunned meat may be imported to Denmark, and Danish stunned meat is exported to some countries in the Middle East.
Finland: Cutting and stunning must happen simultaneously during ritual slaughter. In Åland, pre-cut stunning is required.
France: Restrictions on ritual slaughter are permissible, but only if they do not prevent religious adherents from obtaining religiously slaughtered meat.{{citation needed|date=June 2018}}
Germany: Islamic unstunned slaughter was banned in 1995, but legalised again in 2002. It is illegal to export unstunned meat.
Greece: Animals other than poultry require post-cut stunning during ritual slaughter.
Lithuania: Lithuania legalised unstunned ritual slaughter in 2015 in the midst of a trade war with Russia.
Luxembourg: Religious exemptions to the 1995 law to stun all animals before slaughter became available in 2009.
Netherlands: Since 2011, a veterinarian must be present and since 2018, the animal must lose consciousness within 40 seconds, otherwise stunning is required.
Poland: A 2013 ban on unstunned slaughter on animal rights grounds was overturned in 2014 on religious freedom grounds.
Slovenia: In 2012, Slovenia amended its Animal Welfare Act to ban all forms of ritual slaughter.
Spain: Stunning requirements are dropped if these are "inconsistent with the rules of the respective religious rite".
Sweden: Only stunned slaughter is allowed; some Islamic slaughterhouses in Sweden consider this halal.
